books.section: Topic 8.2 The Cold War from 1945 to 1980
America in an Era of Turmoil (1960-1975)
Unit 8: The Postwar Period and Cold War (1945-1980)

primary_sources: John F. Kennedy, inaugural address, January 20, 1961
Joint Communique of the United States and the People's Republic of China, February 28, 1972
Jimmy Carter, State of the Union address, January 23, 1980

stimulus.source_note: DBQ: documents below are the stimulus.

source: original; documents are paraphrases of public sources (see each document's sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which American Cold War policy changed between 1960 and 1980.

documents.title: Kennedy's inaugural address
documents.source: John F. Kennedy, inaugural address, January 20, 1961. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: Kennedy, speaking at his inauguration at the height of the Cold War, setting out his foreign policy to the nation and the world. Paraphrased from the address.
documents.text: Kennedy promised that the United States would pay any price, bear any burden, and meet any hardship to defend liberty, and he called on Americans to ask what they could do for their country rather than what their country could do for them.

documents.title: Kennedy in West Berlin
documents.source: John F. Kennedy, address in West Berlin, June 26, 1963. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: Kennedy, speaking to a crowd in West Berlin two years after the Wall was built, showing American support for the divided city. Paraphrased from the address.
documents.text: Kennedy told the crowd that he was proud to stand with them in West Berlin, and he called the city a symbol of freedom standing behind a wall that divided it from the Communist East.

documents.title: The Shanghai Communique
documents.source: Joint Communique of the United States and the People's Republic of China (Shanghai Communique), February 28, 1972. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: The joint statement issued at the end of Nixon's visit to China, the first by an American president, setting out how the two governments would deal with each other. Paraphrased from the communique.
documents.text: The two sides agreed that neither should seek dominance in Asia and that both would work toward normal relations, despite their sharp differences over Taiwan and the future of the region.

documents.title: SALT I limits nuclear arms
documents.source: Strategic Arms Limitation Talks, Interim Agreement and Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty, May 26, 1972. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: The first arms-control agreements between the superpowers, signed in Moscow by Nixon and Brezhnev, setting limits on missiles and defenses. Paraphrased from the agreements.
documents.text: The agreements froze the number of long-range missile launchers each side could keep and sharply limited defenses against missiles, so that neither side could shield itself and strike first without fear of reply.

documents.title: The Helsinki Final Act
documents.source: Helsinki Final Act, signed August 1, 1975, by the United States, the Soviet Union, and thirty-three other nations. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: The closing document of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe, signed by President Ford among others, covering borders, trade, and human rights. Paraphrased from the act.
documents.text: The thirty-five nations recognized Europe's existing borders, promised to settle disputes peacefully, and pledged to respect human rights and fundamental freedoms, including the freedom of thought and religion.

documents.title: The Carter Doctrine
documents.source: Jimmy Carter, State of the Union address, January 23, 1980. Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: Carter, speaking to Congress weeks after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, declaring a new American commitment in the Persian Gulf. Paraphrased from the address.
documents.text: Carter declared that any outside attempt to gain control of the Persian Gulf region would be treated as an attack on the vital interests of the United States, and that it would be repelled by any means necessary, including military force.

documents.title: Apollo 11: Aldrin on the Moon
documents.source: NASA photograph, Apollo 11, July 20, 1969. Public domain (PD-USGov-NASA), via Wikimedia Commons.
documents.sourcing: A NASA photograph from the Apollo 11 Moon landing, taken by Neil Armstrong, showing the space race's most famous image at the height of the Cold War.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which American Cold War policy changed between 1960 and 1980, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as containment under Truman and Eisenhower, the arms race, or the Vietnam War and its costs.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about change in Cold War policy.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962, the opening of relations with China in 1979, or the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of change, explaining why change was uneven, or connecting the 1960s and 1970s to the Cold War's end.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: American Cold War policy changed greatly between 1960 and 1980, moving from Kennedy's pledge to bear any burden against communism to Nixon's negotiation with Communist powers and Carter's return to confrontation, though the goal of blocking Soviet expansion never changed.
Context: By 1960 containment was settled policy, tested in Korea and Berlin, and both superpowers held nuclear arsenals that could destroy each other. The Vietnam War then strained American power and public support for the Cold War consensus.
Evidence: Documents 1-2 show the early 1960s stance, Kennedy's pledge and his stand in Berlin. Documents 3-5 show detente, the China opening, SALT I limits, and the Helsinki promises. Document 6 shows the turn back, Carter's warning over the Persian Gulf. Document 7 shows the space race, a contest that ran through the whole period.
Beyond the documents: The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 showed the early policy at its most dangerous, while the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 ended detente and brought sanctions and a military buildup.
Sourcing: Kennedy's inaugural is a public pledge meant to rally the nation, so its boldness is partly performance. The Carter Doctrine is a warning spoken to Congress after an invasion, so its force comes from the crisis behind it.
Complexity: The change was in method, not in goal. Negotiation replaced confrontation for a decade, then confrontation returned, and the same presidents who negotiated also kept the alliances and the arsenals that made negotiation possible.
